newsitem.title: CANADA: Debt-ridden Rogers attacks cash problems with sale.
newsitem.headline: Debt-ridden Rogers attacks cash problems with sale.

text.p: Debt-laden cable television and cellular telephone company Rogers Communications Inc. took a big step toward tackling its cash problems on Wednesday when it signed a deal to sell some Ontario cable systems for C$350 million ($259 million).

The sale to Quebec-based Cogeco Cable Inc. involves systems serving 300,000 subscribers in Hamilton, Niagara Falls, St. Catharines, Sarnia, Wallaceburg, Peterborough, the Ottawa Valley, Cornwall and North Bay.
Most of these systems were acquired in the 1994 takeover of Maclean Hunter Ltd.

Cogeco Cable will pay about C$300 million ($222 million) of the proceeds in cash when the deal closes on Nov. 15. One-third of the balance will be paid to Rogers in the form of subordinate voting shares, subject to stock exchange approvals.
The remaining two-thirds of the price will be in the form of notes payable over the ensuing two years.
Rogers will continue to manage the systems pending approval of the deal by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission, the companies said.
This is Rogers' latest sale from the former Maclean Hunter portfolio.

It also recently realised C$260 million ($192 million) from the sale of 63 percent of tabloid newspaper publisher Toronto Sun Publishing Corp. and C$150 million ($111 million) from the sale of two smaller units -- check printer Davis and Henderson and Roanoke, Va.-based printer Transkrit.
This brings to roughly C$760 million ($562 million) the total raised from asset sales in the past few months, including the sale of the cable systems.

The sales were necessary to pump cash into the emptying coffers of Rogers' cable subsidiary, which is in the midst of a massive upgrade and lugging a debt-load of about C$2.4 billion ($1.77 billion) as of June 30. Rogers has total debt of C$4.7 billion ($3.48 billion).
Rogers Vice-Chairman Phil Lind said in a telephone interview that the cable systems sale should mark the end of significant asset sales by the company.

"We certainly don't anticipate selling any further assets," Lind said, adding that some small sales may be in the offing in the medium-term. He said the proceeds will go directly to cable to help offset the significant cost of the cable rebuild.
Analysts had been anticipating some sort of sale of non-core cable systems, but this deal was on a much larger scale than the market had expected.
